questions.enonce_markdown:
Critically establish the features that characterised the call of Abraham.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** In the Jewish Bible (Old Testament) the call of Abraham (Abram, son of Terah) opens the story of the chosen people. It is reported mainly in Genesis 12:1-3 and is renewed in Genesis 15 and 17. To "establish the features critically" means to identify the main characteristics of the call and to weigh them, noting both their strengths and the points that raise questions.

**1. The call was a divine initiative.** Abraham did not seek God; God spoke first: "Go from your country, your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you" (Genesis 12:1). The call came to a man who lived in an idolatrous setting (Ur of the Chaldeans, then Haran), so it marks a new beginning in God's dealings with humanity after Babel (Genesis 11).

**2. It demanded a radical break with the past.** Abraham had to leave land, clan and security for a destination that was not even named. The call is therefore a test of trust: he was asked to give up everything visible in exchange for a word.

**3. It was accompanied by a threefold promise.** God promised (i) a land, (ii) a great nation, although Sarah was barren and the couple old, and (iii) a great name and blessing. The promises were later sealed in the covenant ceremony of Genesis 15 and in the covenant of circumcision of Genesis 17, where Abram became Abraham, "father of a multitude".

**4. It had a universal purpose.** "In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed" (Genesis 12:3). The election of one man was not meant to exclude others but to serve as a channel of blessing for all peoples.

**5. It called for faith and obedience.** "So Abram went, as the Lord had told him" (Genesis 12:4). Genesis 15:6 says that Abraham "believed the Lord, and he reckoned it to him as righteousness". The New Testament later takes him as a model of faith (for example Hebrews 11).

**Critical assessment.** The call was not without difficulty. Abraham's obedience was incomplete or hesitant at times: he took his nephew Lot with him, he passed Sarah off as his sister in Egypt (Genesis 12:10-20), and he and Sarah tried to fulfil the promise through Hagar (Genesis 16). The promises were also long in being fulfilled: Abraham lived as a sojourner and saw only the beginning of their realisation. These weaknesses show that the call rests on God's faithfulness and not on human perfection, which is exactly why it is remembered as the foundation of Israel's faith.

**Conclusion.** The call of Abraham was characterised by divine initiative, a demand for total trust, a threefold promise of land, descendants and blessing, a universal horizon and a response of faith that was real though imperfect. It forms the basis on which the later history of Israel, from Isaac and Jacob to Moses and David, is built.
